dimensions.form: Singular/plural morphology on nouns; agreement on demonstrative determinatives, verbs, pronouns
dimensions.distribution: Nouns, determinatives, verbs, pronouns; agreement domain extends across clause

1.details: Core semantic features relating to quantity/cardinality of referents

2.details: Indicates whether referents are construed as countable units

3.definition: Encodes the tight/loose hierarchy of count diagnostics
3.details: Tight diagnostics (a/an, low cardinals, distributives) require higher individuation precision than loose diagnostics (many, high round numerals, plural agreement).

stabilisers.evidence: need to track individuation and plurality in discourse

projection.target: The standard count singular three-hour span contrasts with three hours is enough, where a morphologically plural measure can take singular agreement. This rules out deriving all agreement directly from the number of units in the situation.
projection.evidence: CGEL treats amount agreement as an override alongside the ordinary singular and plural agreement construction.

perturbations: reduced transmission or contact leads to erosion of number marking

variation.speaker_variation: register and dialect differences in agreement

coupling.mechanism: bidirectional inference between construal and morphosyntax

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional; singular form cues singular construal, singular construal licenses singular form
Bidirectional; plural form cues non-singular construal, non-singular construal licenses plural form

curious.title: One or more than one
curious.summary: Nouns like cat change form to show one thing or more than one, and words nearby change to match.
curious.body: Cat and cats show one against more than one, and this and these do the same for the word pointing at it. The verb can follow along too. The pattern is about more than counting. Rice and rices show that a word can be treated as something you can count or as an amount you can't, and the choice shows up in the grammar. Some words sit in between: many cattle is fine, while three cattle isn't. In three hours is enough, a plural measure takes a singular verb, so the grammar doesn't just tally the units.
curious.try: Say There's a cat in the garden and then change cat to cats. What else in the sentence has to change?

teacher.summary: Covers singular and plural marking, agreement, and the count/non-count boundary, including odd cases like three hours is enough.
teacher.explain: Grammatical number covers singular and plural morphology on nouns and agreement on demonstrative determinatives, verbs and pronouns. It also reflects whether a referent is construed as countable: rice against rices shows non-count against count construal. This dictionary ranks count diagnostics: the tight ones (a/an, low cardinals, distributives) need more individuation precision than the loose ones (many, high round numerals, plural agreement). Quasi-count nouns show the ranking, as in many cattle against three cattle. Amount agreement is a further override: three hours is enough has a plural measure with singular agreement, so agreement doesn't follow directly from the number of units. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Demonstrative determinatives are this/these and that/those. Non-count is the CGEL term (traditionally mass). Cattle, police and furniture are listed as boundary items.
watch_for: A learner might take plural form to guarantee plural agreement, as in three hours is enough.
A learner might assume a noun that works with the loose diagnostics also works with low cardinals, as with cattle.
teacher.activity: Give students cards with nouns (cat, rice, furniture, hours). They test each with a/an, three, many and a verb, record what works, and sort the nouns into groups.

child.hook: How can you tell one cat from more than one cat?
child.explain: Nouns like cat change when there's more than one. One cat becomes two cats. Words nearby can change too, like this cat and these cats.
child.play: Pick five things in the room and say each as one and as more than one. Then say this or these in front of each.
